These hypotheses come from my prior knowledge of NAS-Bench-201 behavior, not from querying the benchmark. In this space, conv ops dominate accuracy, direct edges from input to output (edge 3) matter as skip routes, and 'none' edges reduce capacity.

1. Setting edge 3 (0→3) to skip_connect helps less when edge 5 is already nor_conv_3x3, because a strong path into the output already supplies the gradient and identity route.
2. Setting edge 0 (0→1) to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 4 (1→3) is nor_conv_3x3, because the feature extracted at node 1 is then used by a strong downstream conv.
3. Setting edge 0 to none hurts more when edge 1 is none, because the cell then has fewer routes from the input.
4. Setting edge 5 (2→3) to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 is nor_conv_3x3, because capacity from a parallel conv path gives diminishing returns.
5. Setting edge 1 (0→2) to nor_conv_1x1 helps more when edge 1 currently has none, because the edit replaces a removed edge, so it adds capacity rather than swapping one conv for another.
6. Setting edge 4 (1→3) to avg_pool_3x3 has a more negative effect when edge 4 currently has nor_conv_3x3, because the edit removes a strong conv rather than replacing a weak op.
7. Setting edge 2 (1→2) to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 0 is nor_conv_3x3, because a deeper conv chain 0→1→2 benefits when the first hop already extracts features.
8. Setting edge 3 to none hurts more when edge 5 is none, because the input then loses its main shortcut to the output and no alternative route remains.
9. Setting edge 3 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 currently has skip_connect than when it currently has none, because replacing a useful skip loses the identity benefit while the conv adds capacity.
10. Setting edge 1 to skip_connect helps less when edge 3 is skip_connect, because a second identity route adds little beyond the first.
